title: Ordering Chai at a Kiosk
culturalNote: Chai (tea) in Kenya is almost always boiled with milk and sugar — strong and sweet. Roadside kiosks (vibanda) are everywhere, serving chai alongside mandazi (fried doughnuts) or mkate (bread). Ordering is quick and informal.

vocabulary.exampleContext: Direct request to the server at a kiosk
vocabulary.sanifuNote: Kenyans commonly drop 'tafadhali' (please) in casual orders — it's implied, not rude
Same drop of 'tafadhali'; the counting word 'moja' is identical in both registers

vocabulary.exampleContext: Added when you don't want the default very-sweet chai
vocabulary.sanifuNote: 'Sukari kidogo' is identical in both registers; Kenyan chai is traditionally very sweet so this signals a preference

vocabulary.exampleContext: If you want unsweetened chai — this will surprise the server
vocabulary.sanifuNote: Identical — 'bila' (without) is standard Swahili used in both registers

vocabulary.exampleContext: Mandazi are fried dough snacks, served with chai
vocabulary.sanifuNote: Kenyans drop the verb clause 'unataka' (you want) — context makes it understood
Direct form, same structure — dropping 'tafadhali' is standard in quick transactions

vocabulary.exampleContext: A polite compliment to the server — appreciated and common
vocabulary.sanifuNote: Identical in both registers — a universal compliment

exercises.prompt: How would you order one tea with a little sugar?
